newsitem.title: BURMA: Detention of Suu Kyi aide prompts fresh protests.
newsitem.headline: Detention of Suu Kyi aide prompts fresh protests.

text.p: Burma said on Thursday that a top official in Aung San Suu Kyi's democracy party was still being held for questioning as fresh condemnation of the ruling junta began pouring in from around the world.

Kyi Maung, deputy chairman of Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy (NLD) party and a close adviser to the Nobel Peace laureate, was picked up on Wednesday for his involvement in a student protest this week, a senior government official said.

"He was picked up early on the morning of the 23rd of October and the reason for calling him in for questioning was because...he met with some of the students involved in a protest for over an hour," the official said in an interview.

The United States and Amnesty International called for the immediate release of Kyi Maung, 75, who was in Rangoon's infamous Insein Prison from 1990 to 1995 for his role in democracy movement activities in Burma.
Washington urged the military authorities to start a dialogue with the opposition on the country's future.

"That's a very disturbing scene to see a peaceful student demonstration turned into a situation where arrests are made (and) people are held without any kind of charge against them," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
"This reflects the brutality of the Burmese government."
Amnesty, the London-based human rights organisation, said Kyi Maung had done nothing more than call for peaceful political change.

"His arrest is an outrage and he should be released immediately. This arrest is part of a relentless attempt by the Myanmar (Burmese) authorities to crush any peaceful dissent by whatever means," Amnesty said in a statement.
Burma's ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) accused Kyi Maung of colluding with some students involved in the street protest on Wednesday morning.
It said he was helping politicise a scuffle that took place on Sunday between students and restaurant owners and trying to create unrest by staging a protest.
A similar scuffle at a tea shop in 1988 sparked nationwide outrage against the military government, leading to pro-democracy street demonstrations that left thousands dead or in jail.

Between 500 and 1,000 Burmese university students staged the rare demonstration against the military government on Wednesday over the way the authorities handled the detention of three classmates involved in the scuffle.

The sit-in protest, staged at an intersection about two km (1.2 miles) from Suu Kyi's home, ended early on Wednesday morning with most of the students going home after teachers and police urged them to disperse peacefully.
Some of the students who did not want to go were escorted back to their residences by police, the government official said, but he added there were no arrests.
The students said official media broadcasts on Tuesday night of the detention of the three students were inaccurate and failed to say the police had manhandled the detainees.
The demonstrators demanded an apology within 48 hours and called for a new media broadcast of the real events.
SLORC said in a statement the demands were impossible and said the students were trying to instigate unrest.
The government has regularly attacked Kyi Maung through official media, saying he was trying to undermine the peace and stability of the nation.
Separately, the European Parliament called for economic sanctions against Burma because of human rights abuses.
In a resolution on Wednesday, the parliament condemned the SLORC for "violations of human rights and fundamental freedoms being perpetrated against the Burmese people."
